title: What the exam builds from these ideas
from: Past exam Questions 2B, 3D, 4B, 5A, 5B, 6A, 6B, 7B and 9, built on lecture notes 10/22 to 11/12
goals: Choose the right alkoxide and halide for a Williamson ether synthesis
Draw an {{SN2}} reaction in which the nucleophile and the leaving group are in the same molecule
Find the hydrogen that can leave in an {{E2}} reaction on a cyclohexane chair
Follow a carbocation through a ring-expanding rearrangement
Use the n + 1 rule to identify an isopropyl group from a septet

sections.title: The Williamson ether synthesis: choosing the right pair (Questions 5A and 6A)
sections.html:
An ether, R-O-R', can be made by {{SN2}}: an alkoxide ({{RO-}}) attacks an alkyl halide (R'-X). This is the Williamson ether synthesis. The name is not in the notes, but every idea in it is. Any unsymmetrical ether can be cut two ways, and the exam asks which way works.

Question 5A. tert-Butyl methyl ether. One pair works:

[[rxn:CC(C)(C)[O-] + CI>>CC(C)(C)OC + [I-]]]

The electrophile is methyl: unhindered, and with no β hydrogen, so elimination is impossible. Even bulky tert-butoxide gets in. The other pair fails:

[[rxn:C[O-] + CC(C)(C)I>>CC(C)=C + CO + [I-]]]

The electrophile is tertiary, so backside attack is blocked: no {{SN2}}. Methoxide is a strong base, so it takes a β hydrogen instead: {{E2}}. The products are 2-methylpropene, methanol and iodide. No ether.

Question 6A. Cyclohexyl methyl ether. Sodium cyclohexanolate with {{CH3Br}} in DMSO is the right choice: a methyl halide can only do {{SN2}}, and DMSO keeps the alkoxide reactive. Bromocyclohexane with {{CH3O-}} in {{CH3OH}} puts a strong base on a secondary halide, and {{E2}} to cyclohexene competes and wins.

[[rxn:BrC1CCCCC1 + C[O-].[Na+]>CH3OH>C1=CCCCC1 + CO + [Na+].[Br-]]]

The rule: make the halide methyl or primary, and put the bulky or secondary group in the alkoxide.

micro.t: Why bulk is tolerated on one partner and not the other
micro.h: In the {{SN2}} transition state the crowding that matters is around the carbon being attacked, because five groups must fit there. Bulk on the nucleophile hurts, but if the electrophile is methyl there is still room (the lecture's homework reaction C, tert-butoxide with iodomethane, works). Bulk on the electrophile is fatal: the lecture's relative rate for tert-butyl is 0. So when one piece of the ether is hindered, that piece must arrive as the alkoxide, with its oxygen already attached.

micro.t: What a full-credit answer to 5A contains
micro.h: From the exam key: the {{SN2}} mechanism for the pair that works, with a backside arrow from oxygen to the methyl carbon and an arrow from C-I to iodine. Then, for the pair that fails: a tertiary carbon cannot undergo {{SN2}} because of sterics; methoxide is a strong base; the {{E2}} mechanism with its three arrows (O lone pair to H, C-H to C=C, C-I to I); and the actual products, the alkene, methanol and iodide. Explaining only why substitution fails, without showing what happens instead, leaves points behind.

macro.t: A reaction chosen by reading the flowchart backwards
macro.h: Until now you have been given reactants and asked for the mechanism. Synthesis runs the other way: you want an {{SN2}} product, so you pick the reactants that land on the {{SN2}} branch of the chart. That means a methyl or primary halide, a good nucleophile, and a polar aprotic solvent. Ether linkages made this way are common in drug molecules, and the same planning question, which partner carries the leaving group, comes up every time one is built.

why.q: Why does swapping which partner is the alkoxide and which is the halide change the outcome completely?
why.a: The alkoxide is both a nucleophile and a strong base, and the halide's structure decides which role it plays. Facing a methyl or primary carbon it can reach, it substitutes. Facing a tertiary or hindered secondary carbon it cannot reach, it removes a β hydrogen and gives an alkene.

sections.title: Intramolecular SN2 and epoxides (Question 4B)
sections.html:
Question 4B: 2-(1-chloroethyl)oxirane with {{CH3O-}} in {{CH3OH}} gives a product in which the epoxide has moved.

[[rxn:CC(Cl)C1CO1 + C[O-]>CH3OH>CC1OC1COC + [Cl-]]]

Analyze the product first. The {{OCH3}} is on the end {{CH2}}, the old epoxide {{CH2}}. The new epoxide joins the old C-Cl carbon and the old epoxide CH. Chlorine is gone. So methoxide did not displace chloride directly.

Step 1: {{SN2}} on the epoxide. Methoxide attacks the less hindered ring carbon, the {{CH2}}, from the back. The C-O ring bond breaks and its electrons go to oxygen. An alkoxide is normally a poor leaving group, but here ring strain is released when it leaves.

[[rxn:CC(Cl)C1CO1 + C[O-]>>CC(Cl)C([O-])COC]]

Step 2: intramolecular {{SN2}}. The new alkoxide oxygen sits one carbon away from the carbon that carries Cl. It attacks that carbon from the back, chloride leaves, and a new three-membered ring closes.

[[rxn:CC(Cl)C([O-])COC>>CC1OC1COC + [Cl-]]]

An {{SN2}} reaction in which the nucleophile and the electrophile are parts of the same molecule is called intramolecular. The arrows are the usual two: lone pair to carbon, C-LG bond to the leaving group. The only new feature is that the product is a ring.

micro.t: The wrong path and how the product rules it out
micro.h: The tempting mechanism is one step: methoxide attacks the C-Cl carbon and pushes out chloride. That would give {{CH3O}} on the secondary carbon with the original epoxide untouched, an isomer of the real product. [[mol:CC(OC)C1CO1]] Compare it with the product given: the {{OCH3}} is on the wrong carbon. Whenever a mechanism question shows the product, number the carbons in the reactant and in the product and see which bonds have changed before drawing any arrow. Here that check is worth 15 of the 50 points.

micro.t: Why an epoxide opens when an ordinary ether does not
micro.h: A three-membered ring has bond angles near 60° instead of 109.5°, and its bonds are eclipsed. The 10/20 lecture gave the consequences for cyclopropane: angle strain plus torsional strain, and a weak, bent C-C bond. An epoxide has about the same ring strain, roughly 27 kcal/mol. Opening the ring releases it, and that pays for making an alkoxide, which would otherwise be a poor leaving group. Under basic conditions the nucleophile goes to the less substituted carbon, as in any {{SN2}}.

macro.h: The reactivity that makes epoxides useful also makes some of them dangerous. Benzo[a]pyrene, a hydrocarbon in tobacco smoke and soot, is oxidized by liver enzymes to an epoxide. A nitrogen atom of a guanine base in DNA attacks the strained ring as a nucleophile and becomes permanently attached to it. That damage can cause mutations. The body's defence is also {{SN2}}-type chemistry: the thiol of glutathione, an excellent sulfur nucleophile, opens epoxides before they reach DNA.

why.q: Why does the alkoxide formed in step 1 attack the neighbouring carbon so readily?
why.a: It is a strong nucleophile held right next to a carbon with a good leaving group, so it does not have to find a partner by collision. It is already in position for backside attack. Chloride is a weak base and leaves easily, which more than makes up for forming a strained ring.

sections.title: Two SN2 reactions that make a ring (Question 6B)
sections.html:
Question 6B: 1,2-diiodoethane reacts with ethane-1,2-dithiolate and gives two products, {{C4H8S2}} and {{C6H12S2I2}}. You are given only the formulas.

[[mol:ICCI]] [[mol:[S-]CC[S-]]]

Each reactant has two reactive ends. The thiolate sulfurs are excellent nucleophiles (compare {{HS-}}, 126,000 in the lecture table). The carbons are primary and carry iodide, an excellent leaving group. Every step is {{SN2}}.

Product {{C4H8S2}}. One sulfur attacks one carbon of the diiodide and iodide leaves.

[[rxn:[S-]CC[S-] + ICCI>>[S-]CCSCCI + [I-]]]

The intermediate has a thiolate at one end and a C-I at the other. The second {{SN2}} is intramolecular and closes a six-membered ring: 1,4-dithiane.

[[rxn:[S-]CCSCCI>>C1CSCCS1 + [I-]]]

Product {{C6H12S2I2}}. If instead each sulfur of one dithiolate attacks a different molecule of diiodoethane, the result is an open chain with an iodine left at each end.

[[rxn:[S-]CC[S-] + ICCI + ICCI>>ICCSCCSCCI + [I-] + [I-]]]

Both products come from two {{SN2}} reactions. The difference is whether the second one happens inside the molecule or with a new partner.

micro.t: Using the formulas as a map
micro.h: Write the pieces: dithiolate {{C2H4S2}}, diiodide {{C2H4I2}}. Each {{SN2}} removes one iodine as iodide. One of each piece, minus two iodines: {{C4H8S2}}. No iodine is left, so both C-I bonds reacted, and there are no charges, so both sulfurs reacted: with two bonds formed between two pieces, the product must be a ring. One dithiolate plus two diiodides, minus two iodines: {{C6H12S2I2}}. Two iodines remain, one on each diiodide unit, so the dithiolate sits in the middle. Formula arithmetic turns an open question into a short one.

micro.t: Why the ring closes so easily
micro.h: In the intermediate the nucleophile and the electrophile are tied together by a short chain, so the sulfur meets the carbon far more often than it would meet a separate molecule. Ring closures that form five- and six-membered rings are especially fast: the chain is long enough to reach the back of the C-I bond without strain, and the ring that forms is strain-free. A six-membered ring with two sulfurs adopts a chair, like cyclohexane.

macro.t: The same step in a chemical weapon and in chemotherapy
macro.h: Sulfur mustard, {{ClCH2CH2SCH2CH2Cl}}, has a sulfur nucleophile two carbons from a C-Cl bond. The sulfur attacks intramolecularly, displaces chloride and forms a strained three-membered ring with a positive sulfur. That ring is a powerful electrophile, and nucleophilic atoms in DNA open it by {{SN2}}. The nitrogen analogues, the nitrogen mustards, react the same way and were among the first anticancer drugs. Each is an intramolecular {{SN2}} followed by an intermolecular one.

why.q: Why does the same pair of reactants give both a ring and an open chain?
why.a: After the first substitution, the remaining thiolate can attack the C-I carbon in its own molecule or the carbon of a fresh diiodoethane. The first choice closes the six-membered ring. The second leaves an unreacted iodide at each end. Which one dominates depends on how much diiodide is around.

sections.title: E2 on a cyclohexane: trans-diaxial or nothing (Questions 3D and 5B)
sections.html:
The lecture's rule is that H and LG must be anti-periplanar. On a cyclohexane chair, two groups on neighbouring carbons are 180° apart only when both are axial, one pointing up and one down: trans-diaxial. An equatorial leaving group has ring C-C bonds anti to it, not hydrogens, so it cannot eliminate.

Question 3D. trans-1-Chloro-2-methylcyclohexane with NaOMe in MeOH.

[[ring:1u:Cl,2d:CH3]]

Draw the chair in which Cl is axial. Because the methyl is trans to Cl, it is axial too:

[[chair:1u:Cl,2d:CH3|A]]

On C2 the axial position is taken by {{CH3}}, so the hydrogen on C2 is equatorial and cannot leave. On C6 there is an axial hydrogen, anti to Cl. The double bond forms between C1 and C6, away from the methyl:

[[mol:CC1CCCC=C1]]

The product is 3-methylcyclohexene, with the methyl still on its dash, because that carbon was not touched. It is not the Zaitsev alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene.

Question 5B. The hexachlorocyclohexane isomer with every Cl equatorial eliminates 7000 times more slowly than any stereoisomer.

[[chair:1u:Cl,2d:Cl,3u:Cl,4d:Cl,5u:Cl,6d:Cl|B]]

Every Cl is equatorial and every H is axial: no Cl has an anti H. Flip the ring and all six Cl become axial, but then every H is equatorial. Neither chair has an axial Cl beside an axial H.

micro.t: The reaction goes through the less stable chair
micro.h:
In Question 3D the more stable chair has Cl and {{CH3}} both equatorial. That chair cannot react. The molecule must first flip to the chair with both groups axial, which is higher in energy (the lecture's A-value for methyl is 1.74 kcal/mol, and chlorine adds a smaller cost), and only a small fraction of molecules are in that form at any moment. The reaction still proceeds, because the chairs interconvert quickly and the reactive one is constantly replaced. Always draw both chairs and ask which one has the leaving group axial.

[[chair:1u:Cl,2d:CH3|B]]

micro.t: Why every other hexachloro isomer is fast
micro.h: In the all-trans isomer, each Cl's neighbours carry their Cl trans to it, so the neighbouring H is cis to it. Cis groups on adjacent carbons are one axial and one equatorial, never both axial. That holds in both chairs, and the all-axial chair is also very strained and hardly populated. Any other stereoisomer has at least one pair of neighbouring Cl that are cis. Then the H on one of those carbons is trans to the Cl on the other, and one chair places them both axial: fast {{E2}}.

macro.h: The compound in Question 5B is a real one: the β isomer of hexachlorocyclohexane, a by-product of making the insecticide lindane (the γ isomer). It is known as the most persistent of the isomers in the environment and in body fat. Its all-equatorial shape makes it the most stable isomer, and, as this question shows, it lacks the trans-diaxial H and Cl needed for easy loss of HCl. Chair analysis of this kind also applies to glucose and to the steroid ring system, where axial and equatorial positions control reactivity.

why.q: Why does trans-1-chloro-2-methylcyclohexane give the less substituted alkene?
why.a: The only chair that can react has Cl axial, and in that chair the trans methyl is also axial, which forces the hydrogen on C2 to be equatorial. The more substituted alkene would need that hydrogen. Only the axial hydrogen on C6 is anti to chlorine, so the double bond forms toward C6.

sections.title: Two eliminations in a row (Question 7B)
sections.html:
Question 7B: 2,3-dibromobutane with 2 equivalents of base gives three products. Two leaving groups and two equivalents of base mean two {{E2}} reactions, one after the other. Each removes H and Br, so the products are all {{C4H6}}.

First {{E2}}. Take the Br on C2 as the leaving group. The β hydrogens are on C3 and on C1.

[[rxn:CC(Br)C(Br)C>base>CC=C(C)Br + C=CC(C)Br]]

Loss of the C3 hydrogen gives 2-bromo-2-butene. Loss of a C1 hydrogen gives 3-bromo-1-butene. (Starting from the other Br gives the same two compounds, because the molecule is symmetrical.)

Second {{E2}}, from 2-bromo-2-butene. The remaining Br is on a double-bond carbon. Its β hydrogens are the vinyl H on the other alkene carbon and the hydrogens of the attached {{CH3}}.

[[rxn:CC=C(C)Br>base>CC#CC + C=C=CC]]

Loss of the vinyl hydrogen gives a triple bond: 2-butyne. Loss of a methyl hydrogen gives two double bonds sharing one carbon: 1,2-butadiene.

Second {{E2}}, from 3-bromo-1-butene. The β hydrogens are on C4 (a {{CH3}}) and on C2 (the vinyl CH).

[[rxn:C=CC(C)Br>base>C=CC=C + C=C=CC]]

Loss of a C4 hydrogen gives 1,3-butadiene. Loss of the C2 hydrogen gives 1,2-butadiene again. Three products in all: 2-butyne, 1,3-butadiene and 1,2-butadiene.

micro.t: A system for not missing a product
micro.h: For each leaving group, list every β carbon and whether it has a hydrogen. Draw the alkene from each. Then treat each intermediate as a new starting material and repeat. Finally, cross out duplicates: here 1,2-butadiene appears twice. A tree like this, with two branches at the first step and two at each second step, gives four paths and three different products. Check the formula of each: {{C4H8Br2}} minus two HBr is {{C4H6}}, and all three answers fit.

micro.t: A vinyl bromide can still eliminate
micro.h: The lecture says vinyl-LG does no {{SN2}} and no {{SN1}}. That is about substitution, where a nucleophile would have to reach the back of an {{sp2}} carbon or a vinyl cation would have to form. {{E2}} is different: the base only needs a β hydrogen, and the electrons of that C-H bond form a second π bond. This is the standard way to make alkynes. It is slower than the first elimination, which is why strong base and two full equivalents are specified.

macro.h: The three products show the three ways to place two π bonds on a four-carbon chain: in one triple bond (an alkyne), in two double bonds separated by a single bond (a conjugated diene), and in two double bonds on the same carbon (an allene, or cumulated diene). They are constitutional isomers. Conjugated dienes are the most stable of the diene types, because their π bonds overlap with each other, and they return later in organic chemistry in the Diels-Alder reaction. 1,3-Butadiene itself is the starting material for synthetic rubber.

why.q: Why does 2,3-dibromobutane give three products when each elimination only removes H and Br?
why.a: At each stage there is more than one β hydrogen that can be removed, and each choice puts the new π bond in a different place. The first elimination can go toward the middle or toward the end of the chain, and the second can again go two ways. The paths lead to an alkyne, a conjugated diene and an allene.

sections.title: Carbocation rearrangements and ring expansion (Question 9 and the 11/10 homework)
sections.html:
The flowchart says it in four words: carbocations can rearrange. A group on the carbon next to {{C+}} moves over with its bonding pair if that makes a more stable cation. The 11/10 homework showed the version that matters here: a cation next to a four-membered ring expands the ring to five.

[[rxn:C[CH+]C1CCC1>>CC1CCC[CH+]1]]

Question 9. An amine next to a cyclobutanol carbon is treated with HONO, which turns the {{NH2}} into {{N2+}} (this is given). Two ketones form, both from one carbocation.

[[mol:CC(N)C1(O)CC2C=CCC12]]

Step 1. {{N2}} leaves (arrow from the C-N bond to N). It is an outstanding leaving group, a stable gas. A secondary carbocation is left, next to the carbon that carries OH, which is part of the strained four-membered ring.

[[rxn:CC([N+]#N)C1(O)CC2C=CCC12>>C[CH+]C1(O)CC2C=CCC12 + N#N]]

Step 2. One of the two ring bonds of the C-OH carbon shifts to the cationic carbon (arrow from that C-C bond to {{C+}}). The ring becomes five-membered, and the positive charge lands on the carbon bearing OH. If the ring {{CH2}} migrates:

[[rxn:C[CH+]C1(O)CC2C=CCC12>>CC1CC2C=CCC2[C+]1O]]

If the ring-fusion CH migrates:

[[rxn:C[CH+]C1(O)CC2C=CCC12>>CC1[C+](O)CC2C=CCC12]]

Step 3. Water removes the O-H proton, and the C-O bond becomes C=O.

[[mol:CC1CC2C=CCC2C1=O]] [[mol:CC1C(=O)CC2C=CCC12]]

micro.h:
First, ring strain. Use the 10/27 table of heats of formation per {{CH2}}, where a strain-free {{CH2}} is −4.9 kcal/mol. Cyclobutane is +1.7, so its strain is 4 × 6.6 = about 26 kcal/mol. Cyclopentane is −3.7, so 5 × 1.2 = about 6. The expansion releases roughly 20 kcal/mol. Second, the new cation is better. The charge moves from a carbon with only alkyl neighbours to a carbon bearing OH, where an oxygen lone pair shares it: {{C+}}-OH is in resonance with C={{O+}}-H, a structure in which every atom has an octet. Losing the proton from that oxygen then gives the neutral ketone directly.

[[mol:CC1CC2C=CCC2C1=[OH+]]]

micro.t: Drawing the shift without losing an atom
micro.h: Number the atoms before you start. Call the cationic carbon a and the C-OH carbon b. Carbon b has two ring bonds, to c (the {{CH2}}) and to d (the ring-fusion CH). In a shift, the bond b-c becomes a bond a-c: the arrow starts in the middle of the b-c bond and ends at a. Now a is bonded to c, and b, having lost a bond, is the new cation. Count the ring: a, c, the next ring carbon, d, b. Five atoms. Repeat with the b-d bond for the second product. Each product is worth 25 points on the key.

macro.h: Carbocation shifts are part of how the body makes cholesterol. An enzyme folds the long chain of squalene oxide, opens its epoxide with acid, and lets a cascade of cations close four rings. The resulting cation then undergoes a series of 1,2-hydride and 1,2-methyl shifts before a proton is lost to give lanosterol, the precursor of cholesterol and the steroid hormones. Each shift follows the rule used in Question 9: a neighbouring group moves with its electron pair to the positive carbon.

why.q: Why does a ring bond migrate in Question 9, when a simple attack by water on the first carbocation would also give a product?
why.a: The shift happens within one molecule and is very fast, and it pays twice: it relieves the strain of the four-membered ring, and it moves the charge to a carbon where an oxygen lone pair can stabilize it by resonance. The rearranged cation is so much more stable that the shift outruns capture by water.

sections.title: Reading a multiplet: what a septet says (Question 2B)
sections.html:
The NMR lecture stops at counting signals. The exam goes one step further and uses splitting. The rule you need is the n + 1 rule: a proton with n equivalent neighbours on the next carbon appears as n + 1 lines.

neighbouring H's (n)lines (n + 1)name
01singlet
12doublet
23triplet
34quartet
67septet

Question 2B. 2-Iodo-2-phenylpropane with NaH gives 2-phenylpropene by {{E2}}. The crude {{1H}} NMR spectrum shows a small septet. What is it?

[[rxn:CC(C)(I)c1ccccc1 + [Na+].[H-]>>C=C(C)c1ccccc1 + "H2" + [Na+].[I-]]]

Seven lines means a hydrogen with six equivalent neighbours. Six equivalent hydrogens next to one hydrogen is two {{CH3}} groups on a CH: an isopropyl group, {{(CH3)2CH-}}. Neither the starting material nor the alkene has one. So the sample contains a little isopropylbenzene (cumene):

[[mol:CC(C)c1ccccc1]]

Some hydride acted as a nucleophile and replaced iodide with H (substitution), instead of acting as a base. Water has no hydride to give, so this by-product cannot form in the water reaction.

micro.t: Where the seven lines come from
micro.h: Each neighbouring hydrogen's nuclear spin is either with or against the magnetic field, and each arrangement shifts the observed proton slightly. With six neighbours, the number of them 'against' can be 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6: seven possibilities, seven lines. The intensities follow Pascal's triangle, 1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1, so the two outer lines are weak and easy to miss. The same isopropyl group also shows its six methyl hydrogens as a doublet (one neighbour, n + 1 = 2). Septet plus a large doublet is the signature of isopropyl.

micro.t: Check the other compounds in the flask
micro.h: Before blaming a by-product, confirm that the expected compounds cannot give the signal. The starting iodide has two equivalent {{CH3}} groups on a carbon with no hydrogen: no neighbours, a singlet. The alkene product has one {{CH3}} and two vinyl hydrogens, with no hydrogen on an adjacent {{sp3}} carbon: again no septet. Only a new compound with a CH flanked by two methyl groups fits, and replacing I by H in the starting material gives exactly that.

macro.t: A spectrum as evidence for a mechanism
macro.h: This question joins the two halves of the unit. The chemistry predicts that hydride, a strong base, should do {{E2}} on a tertiary halide. The spectrum shows a trace of something the prediction left out, and the splitting pattern identifies it well enough to say what the hydride did: a little substitution. The exam key gives 8 points for 'septet = isopropyl CH with six neighbours' and 7 for the inference. The same logic, on protons in the body's water and fat, is the physical basis of MRI.

why.q: Why does the septet point to cumene and not to the starting material or the alkene?
why.a: A septet needs one hydrogen with six equivalent neighbouring hydrogens, which means a CH between two methyl groups. The starting material has iodine, not hydrogen, on that carbon, and the alkene has a double bond there. Only the compound in which H has replaced I has an isopropyl CH.

summary: To make an ether by {{SN2}}, use a methyl or primary halide and put the bulky group in the alkoxide; a tertiary or secondary halide with an alkoxide gives {{E2}}.
An {{SN2}} nucleophile and its electrophile can be in the same molecule, and then the product is a ring, as when an alkoxide closes an epoxide.
Strained epoxides open by {{SN2}} at the less hindered carbon, even though the leaving group is an alkoxide.
A reagent with two nucleophilic ends and one with two leaving groups can react twice, giving a ring or an open chain depending on the partner for the second step.
On a cyclohexane, {{E2}} needs the leaving group axial and an axial hydrogen on the next carbon, and this geometry overrules the Zaitsev rule.
Two eliminations from a dibromide can give an alkyne, a conjugated diene or an allene, so list every β hydrogen at each stage.
A carbocation next to a four-membered ring rearranges by ring expansion, and an OH on the carbon that becomes positive leads to a ketone.
By the n + 1 rule a septet is a hydrogen with six equivalent neighbours: the CH of an isopropyl group.
